analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying forever and stops House members from owning individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in five House committees until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The HUMBLE Act would do several things at once: make former senators and House members permanently ineligible to lobby Congress, strip former House members of perks like chamber access, the members' dining room, and reserved parking, require taxpayer-funded flights to be coach class, bar House members from owning individual corporate stock or sitting on for-profit boards, and dock House members a day's pay for every day a Congress starts without a Speaker. It was referred to five House committees in January 2023 and no committee ever acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who want a Congress less tethered to lobbying firms and personal stock holdings, and current members of Congress who do not personally profit from a revolving door into influence work.

how_it_helps.text: It converts the current one-year lobbying ban for ex-House members and two-year ban for ex-senators into a lifetime prohibition, amending the federal criminal code so any violating contact is punishable under section 216 of title 18 [S3].
It bans House members from owning common stock in individual corporations and from serving on boards of for-profit entities, taking effect January 3, 2025 [S3].
It eliminates taxpayer-funded first or business class airfare for members and legislative staff unless general federal employee rules would allow an upgrade [S3].

It ends former House members' access to the House floor, gyms, members' dining room, and reserved parking unless those are open to the public, with any Speaker-approved waiver published in the Congressional Record within 24 hours [S3].

It would have escrowed House members' pay during the January 2023 Speaker deadlock, holding a day's salary for each day without a Speaker, with the money returned at the end of the Congress to comply with the 27th Amendment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress who sell their access and connections as lobbyists, the lobbying firms that hire them, and members of Congress who would have to move personal investments out of individual stocks and forgo upgraded flights.

drawbacks.text: A total lifetime ban on lobbying by former members is much stricter than the current one- or two-year cooling-off periods, and critics argue it could deter experienced citizens from ever serving in Congress, since leaving office would mean permanently surrendering the right to advise anyone appearing before Congress [S3].

The pay provision is drafted as escrow rather than forfeiture for the 118th Congress specifically to avoid violating the 27th Amendment's rule that member pay cannot change mid-session, so it would inconvenience members without actually costing them money during the Speaker fight it was written for [S3].
The bill applies its ethics restrictions only to the House, not the Senate, and the stock ban would still allow holdings in diversified mutual funds or index funds [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions — a lifetime lobbying ban, a member stock ban, and coach-only travel — directly target the ways members and ex-members can convert public office into private income, and the cost to the public is essentially zero. The lifetime lobbying ban is genuinely stricter than most proposals and raises fair questions about whether it would deter qualified people from serving, but the bill's real weakness was not its design; it was that no committee ever took it up.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees in January 2023 and none of them ever held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on January 25, 2023, the day after the House spent multiple days failing to elect a Speaker [S5][S3].
It was referred to the Committees on House Administration, Judiciary, Ethics, Rules, and Oversight and Accountability, with no action recorded in any of them after the referral [S5].
It drew one cosponsor, a fellow House Democrat, and no further cosponsors over two years [S4].
No roll-call vote was ever held on the bill in the House [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members who lobby Congress, the lobbying firms that hire them, and House members who keep the right to trade individual stocks and use taxpayer-funded premium airfare. Nobody who supported the reform got a vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; the sponsor and sole cosponsor were both Democrats, and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and the revolving-door influence industry
industries.note: The bill would cut off the supply of former members they hire for lifetime access, replacing a one- or two-year cooling-off period with a permanent ban. The industry's business model depends on selling relationships with current members, which is what the public bears in the form of outsized influence.

Ex-members would lose both the right to lobby at any time and their private perks — the House floor, dining room, gym, and parking. These privileges cost taxpayers and give insiders continued access ordinary citizens cannot buy.

industries.industry: Members of Congress holding individual stocks
industries.note: A ban on owning individual corporate stock would force members into diversified funds, removing the conflict of voting on matters that move their personal portfolios.
Restricting official travel to coach would end taxpayer-funded premium seating, saving a small amount of public money and eliminating a member perk.
